newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling continues slide, market nervous.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling continues slide, market nervous.

text.p: The Kenya shilling slid further against the dollar on Thursday as foreign investors pulled out after the IMF cancelled a key aid package to Kenya and ahead of a national strike on Friday.

The shilling fell to a commercial average of about 68.55 at 10.30 a.m. (0730 GMT) from Thursday's close of 67.50 against the dollar -- a decline of 1.55 percent from Thursday and 15.21 percent since the IMF decision a week ago.

One bank quoted its selling rate at 71 against the dollar while another quoted it at 70 against the dollar as the Kenyan currency declined to its lowest levels in four years. Buys were expected at those levels.
The Central Bank of Kenya lists the all-time low rate at 69.22 but commercial banks say a central bank instrument that put premium on the dollar in October 1993 meant real market rates reached 83.
Floor dealers at the Nairobi Stock Exchange said bonds, in which foreign investors hold a huge stake, were under pressure.
"Things are looking very bleak. There's more bonds coming through today (Thursday) because foreigners are still selling," a floor dealer from a leading brokerage firm told Reuters.
"There's an indication that up to one billion shillings of government treasury bonds will be offloaded if the market can absorb them," he added.
Commercial bank dealers said they were taking no chances and would maintain wide spreads to protect their positions.

"The shilling is still looking weak. Big orders are still there and since we're seeing support from the Central Bank of Kenya at top levels, we can only top it up," a senior dealer from a leading commercial bank told Reuters.

Last Thursday, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million three-year aid package under the soft-lending Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF) to Kenya in a row over corruptiom.

On Wednesday, Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem appealed to foreign exchange participants to trade "in an orderly manner so that losses arising from the panic and speculative transactions would be minimised."
Commercial bank dealers said that despite the appeal they could do little when the shilling was under intense pressure.

Commercial dealers said on Wednesday investors were alarmed by President Daniel arap Moi playing down the IMF ruling and urging Kenyans to become self-reliant. He also said the lost IMF loans were insignificant compared to Kenya's whole economy.

An opposition-backed coalition pressing for constitutional reforms has called a national strike for Friday. Some opposition groups have broken ranks with the group, saying dialogue ought to be given a chance. ($1=68.55)
